questions.stem: A client has tetany and other severe symptoms from confirmed hypocalcemia. Which treatment should the nurse anticipate for urgent correction?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Oral calcium alone because severe neuromuscular symptoms do not require rapid calcium replacement","B":"Intravenous calcium, commonly calcium gluconate, with appropriate cardiac and clinical monitoring","C":"Intravenous potassium chloride because potassium replacement directly corrects symptomatic hypocalcemia","D":"Loop diuretic therapy alone because increasing urinary calcium loss rapidly restores serum calcium"}}
questions.rationale: Severe symptomatic hypocalcemia requires prompt intravenous calcium; calcium gluconate is commonly used. Cardiac monitoring is appropriate during IV treatment because rapid calcium administration can affect cardiac conduction.
questions.source_detail: Treatment/Management: IV calcium for severe symptoms, prolonged QT, or acute hypocalcemia; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: A client has recurrent torsades de pointes associated with a prolonged QT interval. Which statement about IV magnesium is accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Routine magnesium is recommended for every polymorphic VT episode even when the QT is normal","B":"Magnesium replaces immediate unsynchronized shock when sustained polymorphic VT is unstable","C":"Magnesium may be considered to suppress recurrent torsades associated with long-QT polymorphic VT","D":"Magnesium is contraindicated in torsades because it predictably lengthens ventricular repolarization"}}
questions.rationale: Current AHA adult advanced life support guidance recommends immediate unsynchronized shock for sustained polymorphic VT. Magnesium may be considered for recurrences of polymorphic VT associated with long QT (torsades), but routine magnesium is not recommended when the QT is normal.
questions.source_name: American Heart Association — 2025 Adult Advanced Life Support
questions.source_detail: Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia section: shock for sustained polymorphic VT; magnesium may be considered for recurrent torsades with long QT; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: A client takes an ACE inhibitor and spironolactone and also uses a potassium-chloride salt substitute. Which complication is the priority concern?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Hypocalcemia because potassium-containing salt substitutes prevent intestinal calcium absorption","B":"Hypokalemia because combining an ACE inhibitor with spironolactone causes excessive potassium loss","C":"Hypernatremia because spironolactone directly increases sodium retention when combined with an ACE inhibitor","D":"Hyperkalemia because the medicines and potassium-containing salt substitute can all raise potassium"}}
questions.rationale: ACE inhibitors can increase serum potassium, and spironolactone is potassium-sparing. Potassium supplements or potassium-containing salt substitutes add further risk, so serum potassium and renal function require monitoring.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Spironolactone Tablets, Warnings and Precautions 5.1 Hyperkalemia
questions.source_detail: Current label accessed 2026-08-14: hyperkalemia risk increases with potassium supplements, potassium-containing salt substitutes, and drugs that increase potassium such as ACE inhibitors; serum potassium monitoring is required.

questions.stem: A client with chronic kidney disease receives an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent. Why should an unnecessarily high hemoglobin target be avoided?

questions.stem: Before IV alteplase for acute ischemic stroke, which finding is a labeled contraindication rather than merely a factor requiring individualized risk assessment?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Active internal bleeding present at the time thrombolytic treatment is being considered","B":"A remote history of uncomplicated surgery with complete healing and no current bleeding","C":"Well-controlled diabetes mellitus without current hemorrhage or other exclusion criteria","D":"Older age by itself without an intracranial bleed, active bleeding, or severe hypertension"}}
questions.rationale: Current Activase labeling lists active internal bleeding as a contraindication for acute ischemic stroke. It also lists current intracranial hemorrhage, subarachnoid hemorrhage, recent intracranial/intraspinal surgery or serious head trauma, bleeding diathesis, and severe uncontrolled hypertension. Recent major nonintracranial surgery is addressed as a bleeding-risk circumstance rather than being equivalent to every absolute contraindication.
questions.source_detail: Contraindications 4.1 Acute Ischemic Stroke and Warnings 5.1 Bleeding; current DailyMed label accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: A client with diabetes who is prone to hypoglycemia starts a beta blocker. Which safety teaching is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Beta blockers cause no clinically important change in hypoglycemia recognition or glucose response","B":"Beta blockers reliably prevent hypoglycemia, so glucose monitoring can usually be reduced substantially","C":"Beta blockers can mask adrenergic warning signs and some agents may prolong or worsen hypoglycemia","D":"Diabetes is an absolute contraindication to every beta blocker regardless of indication or selectivity"}}
questions.rationale: Beta blockers can mask warning manifestations such as tachycardia. Current labeling also notes that severe or prolonged hypoglycemia can occur and that nonselective beta blockade may delay recovery of serum glucose. Patients at risk require monitoring rather than blanket avoidance of the class.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Metoprolol Tartrate / Beta-Blocker Hypoglycemia Warning
questions.source_detail: Warnings and Precautions 5.6 Hypoglycemia: masking tachycardia and risk of severe or prolonged hypoglycemia; current label accessed 2026-08-14.
